title: Make History More Searchable: A Two-Person Transcription Session
subtitle: A digitized page is only the beginning. With a little patience and a partner, you can help make historical records easier for others to read, find and use.
imageAlt: Two friends sit beside one another at a table, comparing a digitized handwritten page on a laptop with its transcription on screen.
imageConcept: Two friends at a kitchen table, one following a digitized manuscript on a laptop while the other checks a draft transcription; the shared focus is on the page, with a notebook and tea nearby.
body:
A collection can be digitized and still be hard to use. A photograph of a handwritten letter lets you see the original, but searching its words or reading it with assistive technology may be difficult. Transcription helps bridge that gap: a volunteer turns the words visible in a digital image into text that people can read, search and study more readily. At the Library of Congress, the By the People program invites volunteers to transcribe, review and tag digitized pages [2]. Completed campaign transcriptions are typically published alongside their images, where they can support searching and use with screen readers [1].

That makes transcription a particular kind of cultural participation. It is not simply looking at an old document, and it is not a claim to interpret its whole meaning. It is careful access work: helping a source become more usable while leaving the source itself intact. A short session with a friend can be a welcoming way to take part, even if neither of you has archival experience.
Choose a page you actually want to meet

Start with curiosity, not an obligation to tackle the most important-sounding material. The Library’s digitized collections include materials from divisions such as the American Folklife Center, Music Division and Manuscript Division, as well as personal archives, writers’ work, and documentation of music and traditions [1]. Browse the active By the People campaigns together and choose a topic that genuinely interests you. A connection to a place, an occupation, a period of history or a question you have both wondered about can help you stay engaged when the handwriting gets difficult.

For a first try, choose a short page rather than setting a word-count goal. Check that the campaign is open and read its instructions before you begin. Campaigns can differ in what they ask volunteers to transcribe, review or tag, so the task shown on the page—not a general assumption about how transcription works—should guide you. By the People says an account is not required just to transcribe, which can make it easier to test the activity before deciding whether to take on more [2].
Set up a session that leaves room to think

You do not need special equipment: a computer or tablet with internet access, a comfortable place to sit, and enough time to read carefully are a good start. Put the document image and its instructions where both people can see them. If the screen is small, use a larger display or take turns zooming in; the aim is to inspect the image, not to race through it.

Agree on a modest first session. The Library’s event guide describes in-person, online and hybrid formats, and suggests that a hosted transcribe-a-thon can run for 1.5 to 3 hours [3]. A pair trying one page does not need to make an event of that length: set aside perhaps 30 minutes, with permission to stop sooner. One person can read the visible text aloud while the other follows the image and checks the draft; then switch. The guide recommends pair and small-group activities, making this shared approach a natural way to practice together [3].
Read what is there, not what you expect

Handwriting invites the eye to complete a word before it has really been read. Slow down at names, dates and unfamiliar terms. Compare the shape of a doubtful letter with the same writer’s other letters on the page. Look at the words around it, but do not let context turn a guess into certainty. If you cannot resolve a word, follow the campaign’s directions for marking uncertainty rather than inventing a reading.

Keep the document’s language as it appears. Old spelling, unusual grammar or inconsistent punctuation can feel like errors to a modern reader, but a transcription is meant to represent the source, not quietly rewrite it. Do not add information that seems likely but is not visible, and do not silently repair a sentence because you think you understand what the writer meant. When the instructions leave a question open, pause and consult the campaign’s guidance. Accuracy includes being honest about what you cannot make out.
Make review a conversation, not a test

After one person has entered a passage, read it back while the other checks the image line by line. A useful rhythm is to compare a short phrase, pause at anything uncertain, and look again before moving on. Switch roles so each person experiences both tasks: deciphering the marks and checking whether the words on screen match them. The Library’s volunteer process includes review by other volunteers before transcriptions return to the Library’s main site [2]. In a two-person session, that habit of checking is valuable even before anything is submitted.

When you disagree, return to the image rather than making the discussion about who is better at reading handwriting. Zoom in, compare letterforms elsewhere on the page and revisit the task instructions. If the evidence still does not settle the question, use the campaign’s uncertainty process. The goal is not to erase every ambiguity; it is to avoid disguising ambiguity as certainty.
Notice what the page does—and does not—say

Once you have worked through a passage, take a moment to discuss what drew your attention. Was there a place name neither of you recognized? Did a familiar word have a different spelling? Did the page raise a question you would want to investigate? These are useful observations, but keep them distinct from the transcription itself. The words on the page are evidence; your interpretation of their context is a further step.

That distinction helps make a small contribution feel meaningful without asking one document to stand for an entire person, community or period. A letter may show a writer addressing one specific situation; it cannot, on its own, explain everything about the world around it. If you want to learn more, note a question and look for other records or reliable contextual sources afterward. Transcription can open a door to research, but it does not finish the research for you.
Leave the work in a usable state

Before you stop, check the campaign’s page for any unfinished task, review step or submission instruction. If you have made a draft together, make sure you know whether it has been saved or submitted; do not assume that closing the browser preserves it. If you are unsure about a word or instruction, leave a short note for yourselves or use the campaign’s available help resources rather than changing the text to make it look complete.

Then decide what you would like to do next: review another person’s page, return to the same campaign, or simply talk about what surprised you. The Library of Congress describes volunteers as helping make its digitized collections more accessible through transcription, review and tagging [2]. The scale of that work is built from individual acts of attention. A page carefully checked by two people is a small contribution, but it can become part of a larger public resource—and an invitation for someone else to find a story they might otherwise have missed.
